title: He refused a judgeship
hook: reports say Abu Hanifa refused to be a judge for the caliph and was imprisoned

segments.voice: Yesterday, the map of the Hanafi school, and your line: the most followed school. Which city on that map did you stop at longest? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

The offer comes with power. A judgeship, with the caliph's backing, with authority over property and marriages and punishments. The man being offered it is a cloth merchant and a teacher with students of his own in Kufa. And he says no. Then he's asked again, and he says no again. The reports differ on the details, but they agree on the shape: the pressure grew, and so did the price of refusing. Yesterday we saw how far Abu Hanifa's school traveled through courts and judges. Today, the founder himself would not sit in the judge's seat. He refused a judgeship.
screen: `A POST WITH POWER.` → `HE SAYS NO, AND NO AGAIN.` → `THE PRICE OF REFUSING.`

segments.voice: First, what the reports say. His biographers tell of a governor of Iraq who wanted him as a judge and had him beaten when he refused. They tell of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur pressing him again, and of Abu Hanifa being imprisoned. Some reports say he died in that prison. The accounts don't all agree, and historians weigh them differently, so it's fair to say: this is what the reports say. Next, a story people tell. When the caliph pressed him, Abu Hanifa said he wasn't fit for the post. The caliph said, you're lying. And Abu Hanifa answered: then you've just ruled that I'm unfit, because a liar can't be a judge. Whether or not it happened in those words, it shows how he's remembered: quick, calm, and impossible to corner. Then, why refuse at all? There's a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud: whoever is made a judge among people has been slaughtered without a knife. Scholars read it as a warning that judging endangers the soul. A wrong ruling could take someone's home or someone's life. Some pious scholars ran from the post for that reason. Others, like Abu Yusuf, accepted it and tried to do it justly, and the tradition honors them too. Last, the other reason readers see. A judge appointed by a ruler can be pushed by that ruler. Refusing kept Abu Hanifa's judgment his own. The school he built went on to staff courts across empires. He himself, the reports say, would not sit in the seat.
screen: `WHAT THE REPORTS SAY.` · `YOU'VE JUST RULED THAT I'M UNFIT.` · `SLAUGHTERED WITHOUT A KNIFE.` · `KEEPING HIS JUDGMENT HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: The practice: refuse a wrong role. Think of a role someone wants you to take that doesn't fit. Covering for a friend. Taking sides in a family fight. Saying yes to a job that would cost you something you won't trade. Hold it plainly. Then find the sentence you'd use to say no, short and kind, without a speech attached. Say it once in your head. Notice your shoulders as you say it. If the role is right after all, notice that too. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
He refused a judgeship. Reports say Abu Hanifa turned down the post of judge, under pressure from a governor and a caliph, and was beaten and imprisoned for it. Today's word.
Your line: he refused the post. Today, if someone hands you a role that isn't yours, try the short, kind no you found. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslim biographers tell of Abu Hanifa refusing the judgeship under pressure, and of other scholars who avoided the post out of fear of judging wrongly, while honoring those who took it and judged justly.

original.note: Arabic: a judge, the one who decides a case; the post Abu Hanifa refused.

trapdoor: what you thought: refusing a top job is just modesty.
what it means: a judge could wrong someone forever, and a ruler's judge could be pushed by the ruler.
